claims.text: In HEAs containing at least five elements at 5 at.% or more each, superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by valence electron concentration.
Replacing part of an alloying element with an element having a higher valence electron count will increase the alloy's VEC.
A small increase in VEC will increase the density of states at the Fermi level.
Increasing the density of states at the Fermi level enhances Cooper pairing.
Enhanced Cooper pairing raises the superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase solid-solution HEA containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 at.%.
The proposed intervention replaces 2–5 at.% of one element with a higher-valence element while retaining single-phase character.
Baseline and modified alloys should be synthesized and heat-treated under identical conditions.
Superconducting resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements should be conducted under identical environmental conditions for both alloys.
Increasing VEC shifts the electron population at energies near the Fermi level.
The higher-VEC alloy should have a higher Tc than the baseline alloy when processing and environmental factors are controlled.
Phase separation, grain-boundary effects, or impurity phases can mask or alter the effect of VEC on Tc.
The quantitative relationship between incremental VEC changes and Tc may depend on the specific alloy system.
X-ray diffraction can be used to assess crystalline structure and phase constitution in the HEA samples.
Failure to observe a statistically significant Tc increase in a phase-pure modified alloy under controlled conditions would falsify the proposed VEC-controlled mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes alloys with unintended phase changes or impurities because these can mask the VEC effect, but the falsification rule says that a Tc change correlated with such phase changes or impurities would falsify the hypothesis. An out-of-bound sample would normally make the test inconclusive rather than falsify the within-boundary claim.
